summary: The Tayron eHybrid is the long-wheelbase Tiguan's plug-in sibling, and in Australia it arrives as two front-wheel-drive grades sharing a 19.7kWh usable battery good for a claimed 113-116km of WLTP electric range — among the longest of any plug-in hybrid on sale here, and enough that most Melbourne commuters would run it as an EV during the week. Reviewers are consistent about the appeal: a 705-litre boot, DC fast charging and genuinely usable EV range at $62,390, which undercuts a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV Exceed. They are equally consistent about the catch — the battery sits where the third row would go, so unlike every petrol Tayron the eHybrid is a five-seater only, and CarExpert judged it less polished than the smaller Tiguan eHybrid it is based on.
pros: 113-116km of WLTP electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery is the longest in the mainstream plug-in SUV class — a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV claims 86km and a Mazda CX-60 PHEV 76km — and CarExpert covered a 50km loop at an indicated 0.0L/100km on battery alone
705 litres of boot with the pack installed beats a Hyundai Santa Fe Hybrid's 628 litres, and 1,915 litres with the rear seats folded is genuinely van-like for the class
40kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in about 30 minutes) plus 11kW AC is rare on a plug-in hybrid — the Outlander PHEV has no 11kW AC and most rivals have no DC capability at all

Volkswagen Australia's five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, not tied to servicing inside the dealer network, and the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km

Both grades sit below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold and rate 38-40g/km CO2 on the combined cycle, well inside Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car test, so no luxury car tax applies and stamp duty is charged at the flat $8.40 per $200 green rate
cons: The battery occupies the third-row well, so neither eHybrid grade can be had with seven seats — every petrol Tayron from the $48,950 110TSI Life up can, which makes the plug-in the wrong car for the family the nameplate is otherwise aimed at

The 1.7-1.8L/100km label figure assumes you start every trip charged; once the battery is flat it is a 1.5-litre turbo hauling about 1,930kg, and UK testing puts it at roughly 40-45mpg (6.3-7.1L/100km), so the running-cost case collapses for a buyer without home charging
Front-wheel drive only — there is no 4MOTION eHybrid — and NRMA found the 1.5-litre engine feels underdone against the kerb weight once it is doing the work on its own
The 200TSI R-Line asks a $14,160 premium over the 150TSI Elegance for 50kW, a 200kg-higher tow rating and trim, and it crosses the $75,000 mark that the 2027 FBT cap is set at
The plug-in hybrid FBT exemption ended on 1 April 2025, so the novated-lease advantage that made earlier PHEVs compelling no longer applies to this car at all
